children: By Farhan Rafid and Anthony Harrup
Crude oil futures declined Wednesday, retreating from the four-month highs reached on growing concerns about Middle East supplies as the conflict drags on with no solution in sight.
Brent crude oil settled down 2.7% at $105.83 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate lost 3.2% to $102.43 a barrel.

"We are viewing this oil price pullback as corrective and still likely to be followed by fresh multi-year highs," oil trading advisory firm Ritterbusch & Associates said in a note. Concerns regarding supply have increased as disruptions extend to the Red Sea and the Saudi pipeline outage, the firm added.
Wednesday's pullback came amid a strong dollar and elevated Treasury yields, which rose after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates as expected in the first increase since 2023.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported a 640,000 barrel draw in U.S. commercial crude oil stocks for last week, which was smaller than expected, while gasoline and diesel inventories saw builds.

Overall inventories remain tight thanks to strong exports, said David Russell, global head of market strategy at TradeStation. "Today's numbers give some pause to the energy rally, but do little to ease bigger concerns about a supply crunch," he said.

Saudi Arabia is trying to resume partial operations within days on its East-West Pipeline after drone attacks forced its shutdown, though damaged pumping stations could take six to eight weeks to fully repair, The Wall Street Journal reported. The 750-mile pipeline can carry as much as 7 million barrels a day to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, providing an alternative export route when flows through the Strait of Hormuz are constrained.

Saudi Arabian Oil Co., known as Aramco, is also reportedly delaying shipments to some European customers following attacks on the pipeline, forcing refiners to seek replacement cargoes, UOB Global Economics & Markets Research said in a note.

Shipping risks also remain elevated around the region's main export routes. As of Sept. 15, the International Maritime Organization had recorded 80 confirmed maritime incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East since the conflict began.
Risks around Saudi Arabia's western export route have increased as Iran-backed Houthi militants expand their territorial gains around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.

U.S.-Iran tensions also remain elevated. The U.S. military fired 60 to 70 Patriot interceptors and more than a dozen THAAD interceptors last week to counter an Iranian attack on Jordan involving about 20 ballistic missiles, U.S. and regional officials familiar with the matter told The Wall Street Journal.

The disruption in the Middle East is already reshaping Europe's physical crude market. Norway's Johan Sverdrup, a medium-sour crude similar in quality to some Middle Eastern grades, jumped $7.265 a barrel Tuesday to reach a record premium of $19.55 above Dated Brent, according to S&P Global Commodity Insights. European refiners have increasingly turned to Johan Sverdrup as a relatively nearby replacement for Middle Eastern barrels, with shipping risks around Hormuz, stronger Asian demand and delays to Middle East cargoes tightening supplies of sour crude. The Saudi East-West Pipeline shutdown triggered a further rush for replacement barrels in the North Sea, S&P said.
